text: A message from Peking states that deadlock between the Powers and China continues, the former insisting on discussion in the first place of China's demands relative to the Shanghai disorders, while China desires to discuss, simultaneously, the revision of the Treaties and other demands which the Powers consider require a larger conference.

label: text
text: Reuter understands now that the French Parliament has ratified the Washington Treaty as regards China; it is expected the ratifications of the various Powers will be shortly deposited.

label: text
text: The Washington Treaty will then come into force, clearing a way for the Tariffs Conference which the British Government regards as an opportunity for doing something to co-operate with China. As regards further Treaty signed at Washington providing a commission to enquire into the abolition of extraterritoriality, this commission is not yet appointed owing to request for postponement by China and other Powers.

text: The situation continues a deadlock. While nothing has been officially announced it appears that the Chinese Government desires that negotiations regarding the last eight of the thirteen demands, as well as the revision of the so-called unequal treaties shall be taken up simultaneously with the first five demands. It is understood that the Powers insist that the five demands arising directly out of the Shanghai incident be discussed first. Meanwhile agitators continue to urge negotiations with Britain alone.

text: (To the Editor of the China Muit.)

label: text
text: Sir,—It is now perfectly clear that the agitators are out to cripple and, if possible, to destroy the business life of the Colony and that the incidents at Shanghai and elsewhere were used as a cloak to conceal their intent. Having served their purpose, these incidents are no longer referred to at all. This being the case, the path for the Hongkong Chinese to take is also clear. The peace of the Colony is threatened and the sporting thing to do is to rally round the Government to help to preserve law and order and thereby protect their own families. All the foreign sportsmen are doing essential service in some form and it is up to the Chinese sportsmen to fall in line. It is true that Dr. Tso and his helpers have gathered together about a thousand Chinese to volunteer but this number is disproportionate and the South China Athletic Association alone should be able to enlist a few hundred amongst its members to serve as Volunteers or Special Constables. This possibility should be immediately considered by Messrs. Li Yih-tong and Ng Szew-kwong, the energetic Chairman of the two most important Chinese sporting organizations of the Colony.
